key_facts: **Naevus sebaceus** is a congenital hamartoma: a yellow-orange hairless plaque on the **scalp** or face.
Flat at birth, becomes warty and raised at puberty under hormonal influence.
Benign tumours (trichoblastoma, syringocystadenoma) can develop in adulthood; true BCC is rare.
Observe; excision is optional (cosmetic or new nodule). Extensive lesions: think Schimmelpenning syndrome.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A congenital **hamartoma** of the folliculosebaceous-apocrine unit, present at birth in about 0.3% of newborns. It is mostly on the scalp, then the face.

ul: **Post-zygotic (mosaic) HRAS (most) or KRAS mutations.** This is why it follows Blaschko's lines and why the same mutation underlies the syndromic forms.

It changes with hormones in **three stages**: infancy (smooth, waxy, yellow-orange, hairless); puberty (sebaceous glands enlarge, so it becomes thick, verrucous and pebbly, as in the boy in [Case 2](condition:dermatofibroma)); adulthood (secondary adnexal tumours may develop).
**"It must be removed in childhood to prevent cancer"**: malignant change is rare; removal is a choice.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A mosaic **RAS mutation** creates a patch of malformed hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

mech.t: A post-zygotic HRAS or KRAS mutation affects one patch of skin.
Follicles are rudimentary (no hair) and sebaceous and apocrine glands are abnormal.
mech.caption: Sebaceous naevus after puberty: papillomatous surface, enlarged sebaceous glands, immature hairless follicles and an ectopic apocrine gland.

mech.t: Androgens enlarge the sebaceous component, so the plaque thickens.
Benign adnexal tumours may arise within it in adulthood.

histo: Papillomatous epidermis, abnormal immature follicles, enlarged sebaceous glands, ectopic apocrine glands.

ul: Well-demarcated, hairless, yellow-orange or pink plaque, usually oval on the scalp or linear on the face/neck child; skin of colour).
In adults: rough, warty, sometimes with papules or nodules inside it.

**Secondary tumours:** they occur in perhaps 10–20% of lesions, mostly in adults, and **most are benign**. Trichoblastoma is commonest, then syringocystadenoma papilliferum, trichilemmoma, sebaceoma and apocrine tumours. **BCC is rare (<1% in modern series)**, and older reports that called trichoblastomas "BCC" exaggerated the risk. SCC, sebaceous carcinoma and apocrine carcinoma are very rare.

**Syndromic forms:** *Schimmelpenning (linear naevus sebaceous) syndrome*: an extensive, often facial, linear naevus with CNS (seizures, developmental delay, hemimegalencephaly), eye (colobomas, choristomas) and skeletal (rickets from hypophosphataemia, FGF23) involvement. *Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica*: sebaceous naevus plus a speckled lentiginous naevus (HRAS).
Clinical in most cases. Dermoscopy shows yellow globules and a cerebriform/papillomatous pattern.
Biopsy any **new nodule, ulcer, bleeding or rapid change** within a sebaceous naevus.
An extensive or facial lesion with neurological, ocular or skeletal signs needs paediatric referral for syndrome work-up.

ddx.name: Aplasia cutis congenita
ddx.f: Membranous or scarred, atrophic, sometimes a "hair collar"; not yellow or waxy

ddx.name: Epidermal (verrucous) naevus
ddx.f: Warty, brown, not yellow; often off the scalp

ddx.name: Juvenile xanthogranuloma
ddx.f: Dome-shaped orange papule, not a plaque

ddx.name: Linear morphoea en coup de sabre (see Other lumps and syndromes)
ddx.f: Acquired (not congenital), indurated, ivory, with hair loss and a groove; **progressive**

ddx.name: Alopecia areata / tinea capitis
ddx.f: Acquired, with normal skin texture or scale

ul: Explain the natural history and the low (mainly benign) tumour risk. **Observation is reasonable**, and many UK paediatric dermatologists no longer advise routine prophylactic excision.

Elective **excision** (the course answer, often in late childhood or adolescence under local anaesthetic, earlier for facial lesions or under GA) is offered for cosmetic, practical (comb trauma, bleeding) or anxiety reasons. It is a shared decision with paediatric dermatology or plastics.

**Refer:** routine to dermatology for confirmation and discussion. **Sooner** for a new nodule, ulceration or bleeding, which needs biopsy. **Paediatrics/neurology** for extensive or syndromic presentations.
Not IP options: laser, PDT, **topical sirolimus** (case reports only; unlicensed; does not remove tumour risk; specialist-only).

refer.t: A new lump, crust, ulcer or bleeding within a sebaceous naevus: refer for **biopsy**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: A new lump, crust, ulcer or bleeding within a sebaceous naevus: refer for **biopsy**.
Secondary tumours (mostly benign), alopecia patch, cosmetic concern.
Benign lifelong lesion.

pearls: Parents often worry about "cancer". Give the honest figures (secondary tumours are mostly benign, BCC under 1%) and teach them to look for **any lump growing within the patch**.
Teenagers notice the change at puberty. Reassure them it is expected, not malignant.

quiz.q: When should you think of Sebaceous naevus (naevus sebaceous)?
quiz.a: A child with a smooth, yellow-orange, hairless plaque on the scalp, or an adult with a warty plaque there.
A hamartoma of epidermis, hair follicles and sebaceous glands (mosaic HRAS/KRAS mutations); hormones thicken it at puberty.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Recognise, photograph and monitor; discuss elective excision; refer any new nodule, ulcer or bleeding within it.
A new lump or crusted area within the naevus (trichoblastoma, rarely BCC); extensive lesions with eye, brain or bone involvement (syndromic).

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: A new lump, crust, ulcer or bleeding within a sebaceous naevus: refer for **biopsy**.
